cards.statement: A DHCPv4 client selects an offered address by identifying its chosen server in DHCPREQUEST.
cards.explanation: The Server Identifier option names the chosen server, allowing servers to recognize which offer the client accepted.

source.title: RFC 2131: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol

cards.statement: A DHCPv4 client rebinding its lease sends DHCPREQUEST directly to the server that granted it.
cards.explanation: At T2, the client broadcasts DHCPREQUEST so any available server can extend the lease. Contacting the original server belongs to the earlier renewal stage.
cards.misconception: Rebinding contacts the original lease server just like renewal.

source.title: RFC 2131: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol

cards.statement: A DHCPv4 relay uses giaddr to tell the server which client subnet needs an address.
cards.explanation: The relay puts its address in giaddr. The server uses this field to identify the client's subnet when choosing an address.

source.title: RFC 2131: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol

cards.statement: An IPv6 host carries Neighbor Discovery messages in ICMPv6 when discovering routers and neighbors.
cards.explanation: Neighbor Discovery defines ICMPv6 messages for interactions between nodes on a link, including router discovery and neighbor address resolution.

source.title: RFC 4861: Neighbor Discovery for IP version 6 (IPv6)

cards.statement: An IPv6 host identifies its default router from the M flag in a Router Advertisement.
cards.explanation: A host learns default routers from Router Advertisements with a nonzero Router Lifetime. The M flag signals managed address configuration.
cards.misconception: The M flag selects the default router instead of signaling managed address configuration.

source.title: RFC 4861: Neighbor Discovery for IP version 6 (IPv6)

cards.statement: For IPv6 address resolution on a multicast link, a host sends Neighbor Solicitation to solicited-node multicast.
cards.explanation: A host directs the address-resolution query to the target's solicited-node multicast address.

source.title: RFC 4861: Neighbor Discovery for IP version 6 (IPv6)

cards.statement: For SLAAC, an IPv6 host trims its interface identifier to make an advertised prefix fit 128 bits.
cards.explanation: A host ignores a SLAAC Prefix Information option when prefix length plus interface identifier length differs from 128 bits; it keeps the link's interface identifier length.
cards.misconception: SLAAC adapts the interface identifier length to fit an arbitrary advertised prefix.

source.title: RFC 4862: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration

cards.statement: An IPv6 node may run Duplicate Address Detection on an anycast address before assigning it.
cards.explanation: IPv6 nodes must not perform Duplicate Address Detection on anycast addresses, which deliberately identify multiple interfaces.
cards.misconception: Duplicate Address Detection also applies to anycast addresses.

source.title: RFC 4862: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration

cards.statement: An IPv6 host generates temporary SLAAC addresses with randomized interface identifiers.
cards.explanation: Randomized interface identifiers help a host create temporary addresses that reduce correlation of activity over time.

source.title: RFC 8981: Temporary Address Extensions for Stateless Address Autoconfiguration in IPv6

cards.statement: A DHCPv6 relay uses the client's UDP port 546 as its listening port for DHCPv6 messages.
cards.explanation: DHCPv6 clients listen on UDP port 546; servers and relay agents listen on UDP port 547. A relay follows the server-side listening role.
cards.misconception: A relay receiving client messages listens on the client port.

source.title: RFC 9915: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)

cards.statement: A host uses stateless DHCPv6 to request an IPv6 address after processing a Router Advertisement.
cards.explanation: Stateless DHCPv6 provides configuration such as DNS server addresses through Information-request and Reply messages. The host obtains its IPv6 addresses separately.
cards.misconception: Stateless DHCPv6 provides IPv6 address leases.

source.title: RFC 9915: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)

cards.statement: A DHCPv6 client can obtain a prefix to number networks on its downstream links.
cards.explanation: Prefix delegation gives the client address space to manage. The client can divide it into subnets and assign them to downstream links.

source.title: RFC 9915: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)

cards.statement: In IPv4, a host returns the Echo Request's data unchanged in its ICMP Echo Reply.
cards.explanation: The Echo Reply carries the request's data back to its sender, letting the sender compare the response with the data it sent.

source.title: RFC 792: Internet Control Message Protocol

cards.statement: An IPv6 receiver treats an ICMPv6 message with a type below 128 as an error message.
cards.explanation: ICMPv6 divides its type space into error messages below 128 and informational messages from 128 upward.

source.title: RFC 4443: Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMPv6) for the Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) Specification

cards.statement: In IPv4, a host reports an undeliverable ICMP error by sending another ICMP error.
cards.explanation: An IPv4 host suppresses ICMP errors triggered by ICMP error messages, preventing an error exchange from feeding itself.
cards.misconception: ICMP error messages receive further ICMP errors when their delivery fails.

source.title: RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Communication Layers

cards.statement: An IPv6 router resets a packet's Hop Limit when forwarding the packet onto another link.
cards.explanation: An IPv6 router decrements the Hop Limit when it forwards a packet. Resetting the value at each link would defeat the limit on circulation.
cards.misconception: The Hop Limit restarts on each link instead of decreasing across the route.

source.title: RFC 8200: Internet Protocol, Version 6 (IPv6) Specification

cards.statement: Classic traceroute sends successive probes with increasing IPv4 TTL values to reveal router hops.
cards.explanation: A router where a probe's TTL expires returns Time Exceeded. Increasing the TTL lets successive probes reach farther along the path.

source.title: RFC 2151: A Primer On Internet and TCP/IP Tools and Utilities

cards.statement: A sender chooses packet sizes using the largest link MTU along the path as its path MTU.
cards.explanation: The path MTU is the smallest link MTU along the path, because a packet has to fit through its most restrictive link.
cards.misconception: The largest link determines the usable packet size for the whole path.

source.title: RFC 8201: Path MTU Discovery for IP version 6

cards.statement: In IPv4, a router clears the DF flag before splitting a datagram that exceeds its next link's MTU.
cards.explanation: An IPv4 router discards a datagram that needs fragmentation when Don't Fragment is set. The bit prevents routers from splitting that datagram.
cards.misconception: Routers override Don't Fragment to forward oversized IPv4 datagrams.

source.title: RFC 791: Internet Protocol

cards.statement: An IPv4 router must be capable of forwarding a 68-octet IP datagram as one packet.
cards.explanation: The 68-octet forwarding minimum accommodates the largest IPv4 header plus one eight-octet fragmentation unit.

source.title: RFC 791: Internet Protocol

cards.statement: A filter that drops IPv6 Packet Too Big messages can let a TCP handshake succeed while data stalls.
cards.explanation: Small handshake packets may pass while larger IPv6 packets exceed the path MTU. Dropping Packet Too Big prevents the sender from learning the smaller MTU through ICMP-based discovery.

source.title: RFC 8201: Path MTU Discovery for IP version 6

cards.statement: An IPv6 router fragments an oversized packet before forwarding it onto a link with a smaller MTU.
cards.explanation: In IPv6, the source creates fragments and the destination reassembles them; routers leave fragmentation to the source.
cards.misconception: IPv6 routers fragment packets to fit the next link, as IPv4 routers can.

source.title: RFC 8200: Internet Protocol, Version 6 (IPv6) Specification

cards.statement: An IPv6 link must present an MTU of at least 1280 octets to hosts using the IPv6 layer.
cards.explanation: If the underlying link cannot carry 1280 octets in one piece, it supplies fragmentation and reassembly below IPv6 to meet the minimum.

source.title: RFC 8200: Internet Protocol, Version 6 (IPv6) Specification

cards.statement: A DPLPMTUD sender can treat a lost probe as proof that its size exceeds the path MTU.
cards.explanation: DPLPMTUD confirms a usable packet size from successful probe delivery. A lost probe may reflect congestion or a link error rather than an MTU limit.
cards.misconception: Probe loss conclusively identifies an MTU limit.

source.title: RFC 8899: Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery for Datagram Transports

cards.statement: In ordinary IPv4 forwarding, a router replaces the destination IP address with its chosen next hop.
cards.explanation: Ordinary IPv4 forwarding preserves the destination IP address. The router uses a separate next-hop address to send the packet onward.
cards.misconception: Forwarding replaces the packet's destination with the next router.

source.title: RFC 1812, Section 5.2.4: Determining the Next Hop Address

cards.statement: In ordinary IPv4 forwarding, a router can let a lower-metric /16 outrank a matching /24 route.
cards.explanation: A matching /24 wins over a matching /16. The router selects the longest matching prefix before comparing route metrics.
cards.misconception: A lower route metric outranks a more specific matching prefix.

source.title: RFC 1812, Section 5.2.4.3: Next Hop Address

cards.statement: IPv4 routers can forward a reply along a different network path from the packet that prompted it.
cards.explanation: Routers make forwarding decisions independently at each hop. Routing in the reverse direction can lead through different routers.

source.title: RFC 1812, Sections 5.3.8 and 7.4: Asymmetric Paths and Static Routing

cards.statement: BGP speakers advertise IP prefix reachability between Autonomous Systems to build inter-domain routes.
cards.explanation: BGP shares reachable prefixes and paths across administrative boundaries.

source.title: RFC 4271, Section 3: Summary of Operation

cards.statement: A BGP speaker listens for incoming connections from its peers on the registered TCP port 179.
cards.explanation: A BGP peer establishes its session over a TCP connection to port 179.

source.title: RFC 4271, Section 8.2: Description of FSM

cards.statement: BGP treats two peers in the same Autonomous System as external when they sit on different IP subnets.
cards.explanation: BGP peers in the same AS are internal peers, even across IP subnet boundaries.
cards.misconception: Subnet boundaries determine external BGP peering.

source.title: RFC 4271, Section 1.1: Definition of Commonly Used Terms

cards.statement: A BGP speaker appends its AS number to the right-hand end of AS_PATH when advertising to an external peer.
cards.explanation: A speaker advertising externally inserts its AS number before the existing AS_PATH.
cards.misconception: Speakers add their AS after the existing path.

source.title: RFC 4271, Section 5.1.2: AS_PATH

cards.statement: A BGP speaker should exclude a route if its received AS_PATH contains the speaker's own AS number.
cards.explanation: The speaker's own AS in AS_PATH indicates a route has looped back.

source.title: RFC 4271, Section 9.1.2: Phase 2 Route Selection

cards.statement: A BGP speaker can read a measured end-to-end latency metric from RFC 4271's UPDATE attributes.
cards.explanation: BGP applies local policy to path attributes; its UPDATE messages define no end-to-end latency metric.
cards.misconception: BGP advertises measured latency for route selection.

source.title: RFC 4271: UPDATE Message and Decision Process

cards.statement: A BGP speaker can use four-octet AS numbers to identify Autonomous Systems in route advertisements.
cards.explanation: The AS-number extension expands BGP's AS-number space beyond the original two-octet format.

source.title: RFC 6793, Sections 1 and 3: Four-Octet AS Number Extensions

cards.statement: An EBGP speaker uses incoming routes by default before an explicit import policy is configured.
cards.explanation: By default, routes from an EBGP peer are ineligible for selection until the speaker applies an explicit import policy.
cards.misconception: EBGP defaults to using received routes until an import filter is added.

source.title: RFC 8212, Section 3: Changes to RFC 4271

cards.statement: A customer AS that advertises a provider's route to another provider against policy creates a BGP route leak.
cards.explanation: A route leak spreads a learned route beyond its permitted scope. The customer AS can become an unintended transit path.

source.title: RFC 7908, Section 3.1: Hairpin Turn with Full Prefix

cards.statement: A UDP receiver delivers back-to-back received datagrams to the application as separate messages.
cards.explanation: UDP preserves each datagram as a separate message at the receiving application.

source.title: User Datagram Protocol

cards.statement: UDP delivers an application's datagrams in the order in which the application sends them.
cards.explanation: UDP provides no ordering guarantee. A receiver may get datagrams in a different order.
cards.misconception: UDP guarantees datagram arrival order.

source.title: User Datagram Protocol

cards.statement: Each UDP base header has fields for source port, destination port, length and checksum.
cards.explanation: The eight-byte base header carries transport addressing, datagram length and checksum.

source.title: User Datagram Protocol

cards.statement: A UDP sender calculates its checksum independently of the source and destination IP addresses.
cards.explanation: The UDP checksum includes a pseudo-header containing the source and destination IP addresses.
cards.misconception: UDP checksum calculation excludes IP addresses.

source.title: User Datagram Protocol

cards.statement: An IPv6 UDP tunnel may use a zero checksum under the specified tunnel exception.
cards.explanation: UDP over IPv6 normally requires a checksum. Qualifying tunnel protocols follow specified additional requirements to use zero.

source.title: Internet Protocol, Version 6 (IPv6) Specification

cards.statement: UDP reduces an application's sending rate when the network becomes congested.
cards.explanation: Applications using UDP need congestion control in the application or a protocol above UDP; UDP itself supplies none.
cards.misconception: UDP supplies automatic congestion control.

source.title: UDP Usage Guidelines

cards.statement: TCP and UDP use 16-bit port numbers to distinguish services at an IP endpoint.
cards.explanation: The transport layer uses port numbers to direct incoming data to the intended application.

source.title: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry Management

cards.statement: An IANA assignment for a UDP port automatically assigns that number to TCP as well.
cards.explanation: IANA assigns a port for the requested transport protocols and marks it Reserved for the others.
cards.misconception: A UDP port assignment automatically includes TCP.

source.title: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry Management

cards.statement: An operator looking up port 443 in IANA's ranges finds it among the User Ports.
cards.explanation: Port 443 lies in the System Ports range, 0–1023. User Ports span 1024–49151.
cards.misconception: Port 443 belongs to the User Ports range.
tags: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry

source.title: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry Management

cards.statement: IANA keeps the Dynamic Ports range outside the pool of port numbers available for service assignments.
cards.explanation: IANA makes no assignments in 49152–65535; applications use this range locally.
tags: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry

source.title: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry Management

cards.statement: An IANA port assignment allows an operator to prove the application protocol from the port number.
cards.explanation: An assigned port suggests a service, but its traffic can belong to a different application protocol.
cards.misconception: An assigned port proves which protocol its traffic uses.
tags: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry

source.title: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry Management

cards.statement: IANA assigns UDP port 123 to NTP traffic between time-synchronization endpoints.
cards.explanation: The registry lists ntp on UDP port 123, giving operators a standard destination to check for NTP.
cards.appliesTo: IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry

source.title: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry
